title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: man is a real subject with a singular verb, and it is how German says what people do without naming who: Man feiert das Fest im Dezember. Hier geht man um acht nach Hause. English reaches for you (round here you go home at eight) or for a passive, and neither maps cleanly; the stiff English one is not what man sounds like at all — man is completely ordinary, and you should use it without embarrassment. It is also the cheaper of this module's two impersonals, and it carries most of these sentences.

THE PRESENT PASSIVE is werden plus a participle: werden conjugated in position two, the participle at the very END. Das Fest wird im Dezember gefeiert. That is L2-M1's bracket for the fifth time in this course — the same frame that holds a modal and its infinitive, and an auxiliary and its participle — so there is nothing new about the shape, only about what fills it. Every participle it needs is already formed by the rule L2-M10 stated.

werden is a THREE-JOB key and one note is true of all three: to become (Es wird kalt), the passive auxiliary (Das Fest wird gefeiert), and the future auxiliary this course has never needed, because German lets the present do the future's work — Ich komme morgen. When you meet werden, look at what follows: an adjective means becoming, a participle at the end means the passive.

What stays out, because the edge is right here: the PAST passive (wurde gefeiert), the agent named with von (von der Familie gefeiert) and the sein-passive of a resulting state (Die Tür ist geschlossen) all belong to L4-M7, Official talk. This module writes the present passive and nothing else. The past exists and you will see it on a sign; you do not need to build it yet.

Culture is described here, never explained, and no sentence claims a practice for the whole language area: Germany, Austria and Switzerland do not keep one calendar, and the north and south of Germany do not either. That is exactly what man and Hier and Bei uns are for — they say what happens where you are standing, and leave the rest of the map alone.

sentences.display: Man feiert das Fest im Dezember
sentences.cue: People celebrate the festival in December
sentences.literal: one celebrates the festival in-the December

words.note: A subject, not a word for a person: it always takes the er/sie/es verb. Do not confuse it with der Mann, which is a man and is spelled with two n.
feiern, to celebrate, and also simply to have a party. The participle is gefeiert, formed by L2-M10's rule with no surprises.
das Fest, plural die Feste — a festival or any big celebration. A birthday party is a Fest as readily as a public holiday is.
der Dezember, and a month takes im: im Dezember, im Januar. Months are capitalised like every other German noun.

sentences.trap: man is not the English one. One celebrates sounds like a lecture; man feiert is what anybody says at a bus stop.
sentences.sound: man FY-ert das fest im day-TSEM-ber. The ei of feiert is the eye sound; the z of Dezember is ts.

variations.display: Hier feiert man das Fest im Sommer
variations.cue: Here people celebrate the festival in summer
variations.changed: a fronted Hier, so the verb stays second and man follows it

variations.display: Bei uns feiert man zu Hause
variations.cue: Where I'm from people celebrate at home
variations.changed: Bei uns — the same order, and it says where without claiming more

mistake.display: Man feiern das Fest im Dezember
mistake.why: man always takes the singular verb, whatever number of people it means: man feiert.

sentences.usage: Describing what happens around you without naming who does it.
sentences.mnemonic: man is one word and one verb ending: feiert, kommt, geht.

sentences.display: Das Fest wird im Dezember gefeiert
sentences.cue: The festival is celebrated in December
sentences.literal: the festival becomes in-the December celebrated

words.note: werden: to become, and the passive auxiliary. In the passive it stands second and the participle goes to the very end of the sentence.

sentences.trap: English builds its passive on to be — is celebrated. German builds it on werden, to become. Ist gefeiert says something else and is L4-M7's.
sentences.sound: das fest virt im day-TSEM-ber guh-FY-ert. w is said as an English v, and the d of wird as a t.

variations.changed: the same passive on L3-M8's verb — nothing new but the participle

variations.display: Die Feste werden im Sommer gefeiert
variations.cue: The festivals are celebrated in summer
variations.changed: a plural subject, so werden rather than wird

mistake.display: Das Fest ist im Dezember gefeiert
mistake.why: sein plus a participle describes a finished state, not an event. The present passive is wird … gefeiert.

sentences.usage: The written register — a poster, a programme, a notice on a door.

words.note: jeder is singular and takes the singular verb, exactly as man does: Jeder kommt. Before a noun it agrees — jeder Tag, jede Woche.
das Geschenk, plural die Geschenke. Built on schenken, to give as a gift — the ge- here makes a noun, not a participle.

sentences.trap: English everyone comes feels plural — they all come. German jeder is strictly one at a time and never takes a plural verb.
sentences.sound: YAY-der komt mit INE-em guh-SHENK. The J of jeder is a y.

variations.changed: alle instead of jeder, so the verb is plural

sentences.usage: Saying what is expected of a guest, without telling anybody what to do.

sentences.display: Alle Kinder freuen sich auf das Fest
sentences.cue: All the children are looking forward to the festival
sentences.literal: all children gladden themselves onto the festival

words.note: alle is plural where jeder is singular: alle Kinder kommen, jedes Kind kommt. On its own it means everybody.

sentences.trap: German says alle Kinder with no article between them; all OF the children needs no von and no der.
sentences.sound: AL-uh KIN-der FROY-en zikh owf das fest. The eu of freuen is the oy of boy.

variations.display: Alle freuen sich auf den Feiertag
variations.cue: Everyone is looking forward to the public holiday
variations.changed: alle standing on its own as the subject

sentences.usage: M6's reflexive doing its everyday work — the sentence a parent says in the week before a festival.

words.note: viele is a different word from L2-M6's viel: viele counts things (viele Kinder), viel measures a mass (viel Zeit). Both are yours now.
besuchen takes its object straight, with no preposition: Ich besuche meine Eltern. The participle is besucht, with no ge- after be-.

sentences.trap: English visits WITH someone in some places; German never does. besuchen takes the accusative and nothing else.
sentences.sound: FEE-luh KIN-der buh-ZOO-khen EE-ruh EL-tern. The v of viele is an f.

variations.changed: Leute instead of Kinder — the general word for people

sentences.usage: What a holiday looks like in practice, said without claiming it holds everywhere.

words.note: einladen is separable (Ich lade dich ein), so the ge- of the participle lands INSIDE the word: ein-ge-laden. L3-M1's rule, with an irregular vowel in lädt.

sentences.trap: The ge- does not go at the front. A separable verb wraps it: eingeladen, angerufen, aufgestanden — all of them L3-M1's shape.
sentences.sound: ikh HAH-buh AL-luh FROYN-duh AYN-guh-lah-den. The stress sits on the ein.

variations.changed: the present, so the prefix comes off and waits at the end

mistake.why: The ge- belongs between the prefix and the stem: eingeladen. Only an inseparable verb loses the ge- altogether.

sentences.usage: Your own party rather than a public festival — and the sentence that starts one.

sentences.cue: We don't work on the public holiday

words.note: der Feiertag is a day off for everybody, feiern plus Tag. Urlaub is holiday you take yourself, and it is a different word.

sentences.trap: A Feiertag is not a holiday you book. It is a public day off, and which days count differs between the Länder.
sentences.sound: am FY-er-tahk AR-by-ten veer nikht. Feiertag stresses its first syllable.

variations.cue: No work is done on the public holiday
variations.changed: the passive with no subject at all — the register of a notice

sentences.usage: Explaining why the shops are shut, which on a Feiertag they will be.

sentences.display: Es wird im Sommer sehr warm
sentences.cue: It gets very warm in summer
sentences.literal: it becomes in-the summer very warm

words.note: der Sommer, and a season takes im like a month: im Sommer, im Winter. The plural is the same word.

sentences.trap: Here werden is not the passive at all — an adjective follows it, so it means becoming. Es ist warm is the state; es wird warm is the change.
sentences.sound: es virt im ZOM-er zair varm. Both w's are v's, and the S of Sommer is a z.

variations.changed: the shortest version of the same verb, with L1-M9's kalt

sentences.usage: Weather, and the sentence that follows anyone opening a window.
sentences.mnemonic: Adjective after werden: becoming. Participle at the end: passive.

sentences.display: Viele Leute laden ihre Freunde ein
sentences.literal: many people load their friends in

words.note: die Leute is plural only — there is no one Leut. For a single person German says Mensch or Person, and for people in general it says man.

sentences.trap: Leute has no singular and takes a plural verb: viele Leute kommen. Reaching for one person out of it needs a different word.
sentences.sound: FEE-luh LOY-tuh LAH-den EE-ruh FROYN-duh ine. The eu of Leute and Freunde is the oy of boy.

variations.changed: man instead of viele Leute, so the verb is singular — and lädt has the umlaut

sentences.usage: The habit described from the outside, in the register of a guidebook or of small talk.

sentences.display: Man feiert den Geburtstag mit der Familie
sentences.cue: People celebrate the birthday with the family
sentences.literal: one celebrates the birthday with the family

words.note: der Geburtstag — birth plus day. Congratulating anyone before the day is widely avoided; the wish waits until the day itself.
die Familie, said fa-MEE-lee-uh with four syllables. It is singular and takes a singular verb: Die Familie kommt.

sentences.trap: mit always takes the dative, so it is mit der Familie — no motion question to ask, unlike L2-M4's an and auf.
sentences.sound: man FY-ert dayn guh-BOORTS-tahk mit dair fa-MEE-lee-uh. Familie has four syllables.

variations.display: Der Geburtstag wird zu Hause gefeiert
variations.cue: The birthday is celebrated at home
variations.changed: the passive again, with the participle at the end

sentences.usage: Describing the ordinary shape of a birthday where you are, and leaving the rest of the map alone.
